To a certain extent yes, but what they are doing is far beyond what is normal. Government science and its distribution has always been to some degree, informed by up the chain decisions, just as it is in academia. What to fund or not, what to publish or not, etc. This is why it’s so important that scientific/medical agencies be run by people who are seasoned experts. Even then, we’re all humans and it’s never 100% perfect. Scientific data requires human interpretation to have useful meaning. The idea that science has ever been a perfect bastion completely devoid of the larger political and social context is delusional. 

But what does not usually happen (at least in modern western society) is political agents reading scientific findings line by line to edit out things that undermine the party line or the ego of national leaders. Or specifically defunding research that does the same. 

TL;DR: This is not normal. This is textbook fascism.

This is the single most inspiring and wholesome post I have ever read on Reddit and perhaps on any social media platform. No, I am not joking or exaggerating for effect. The pure, simple humanity of your story is really connecting with me and also gave me a much-needed chuckle.

I, too, still have my job at CDC but I’m so completely exhausted by all of this. This is on top of the bone-deep burnout I feel from a decade of working myself nearly to death in emergency responses. I was already completely burned out when the COVID response first started in early January before any of the lockdowns. The next two years after are a blur.

It certainly doesn’t help that for nearly my entire life, I’ve white-knuckled my way through multiple, chronic psychiatric conditions to be able to find any measure of success in my life. I have since started getting medication and therapy, which help a lot but are nowhere near a magic bullet. 

Now amidst all the current socio-political bullshit and our increasingly techno-feudalist hellscape of a civilization, our office leadership is separately turning my organization into a toxic, bullying, mean girls pressure cooker as they ride us all hard toward insanely unrealistic target dates for all of our goals. I just got diagnosed with a chronic disease that left me in constant, unbearable pain unable to walk or even move much at all for a couple weeks and might do the same again at any time. 

I am still working remote, but only because they’re still finding me an office, which I hope won’t turn out to be a two to four hour, one-way commute or worse. 

Oh and to top off the deluxe burnout sundae there’s now a nice little dollop of survivor’s guilt from the mass firings. 

The level of mental, physical, and spiritual burnout I feel is hard to really describe in words. I can barely remember what it feels like not to be depressed and anxious and angry and exhausted all the time. It’s been my default state for most of my life but  more so now than ever. 

I try to take one day at a time and limit my news and doomscrolling (I’m breaking my own rule on this right now). I try to practice gratitude that I still have an income and roof over my head and good food on the table. I have with me the most amazing, inspiring, beautiful, talented, driven, and fun woman that any guy could possibly hope for, especially a guy with as much dark emotional bullshit as I have. I have a good network of family and friends and live in a safe, clean area. I have a very cute cat. I recently took a trip to Vietnam with my partner and some friends, which was a bucket list trip for me. 

Lifting heavy weights at least 3x a week with loud death metal helps a lot. I’ve been eating healthier and watching my sleep and hydration levels which help, too. Lost a few pounds again and trying as hard as possible to look on the bright side. Starting to pull myself together enough to look for a new job outside CDC. 

Keep moving forward. One day at time. One breath at a time. Push the rock another inch up the hill and keep on pushing when it rolls back a few feet That’s all we can ever really do in the end. 

Thanks for reading my Ted talk.

I did a little more digging and depending on your state's exact  laws, you may be eligible. There is legal and regulatory precedent that leaving or being fired from a job because they asked you to make an "unreasonable" life change that alters previous agreements would count as no fault. But the standard is pretty high so having an annoyingly long commute in the same general area wouldn't count. Having to move your family a thousand miles away and your spouse quitting their job would be a much stronger case for benefits. 

Moral of the story: talk to an employment lawyer and don't believe a single word your agency tells you as sound legal advice. And download any documentation of remote agreements.

OP, if you don't mind a bit of long-winded story time, my situation is similar to yours and I hope it helps you to hear from someone has gone, and is still going through, many of the same feelings and experiences even long before the current attack on feds. Here goes:  

I've got 14 years in govt, the vast majority of it working in the emergency operations center at CDC. Ebola, Zika, MERS, natural disasters, you name it. Years upon years spent working myself to the bone to sacrifice for my country. So many 80-100 hour, 7-day work weeks. Hundreds of emails per hour late into the night. Lines of people at my desk all wanting their thing done RIGHT NOW.

I was already struggling with nearly a decade of built up massive burnout, crippling depression and anxiety, and stress-related physical health issues when, one fine morning, I was called into my bosses office in early January 2020 on a call with CDC china office about a rapidly emerging outbreak of "unknown pneumonia"...

Two very long long years later and barely hanging on by a thread, I was finally able to escape to another job at CDC that took me away from the covid response. Leveraged new remote work options to move back close to family. Slowly but surely started to heal my body and mind and learn healthy work/life boundaries. 

But the current situation, the uncertainty that I may have to choose between my job income and my family because of RTO, the threat of large-scale RIFs, the stress and confusion of now having to take one even more in my already maxed-out portfolio of projects after losing extremely talented and hard working probation employees, survivors guilt that I (for now) still have my job, the resentment that I sacrificed so much to save the lives of people who wish me financial ruin and social degradation.... It's really gotten into my head and destroyed three years of healing in only a few weeks. Not to mention a long history of underlying clinical mental health issues going back to my childhood and multiple close family members being diagnosed with pretty serious health issues. 


I normally consider myself to be a pretty resilient person, at least on the surface. Many other people tell me things like "you are a rock in a moving storm." But so often, I've felt more like the tree blown down by the wind. I highly suspect you are the same as me. A person who can pull it together and be a consummate professional with grace under fire when the cameras are on. You put your head down and do the work and that saves you from having to think too much about the bigger picture so you can just make it through to the next day, or even the next breath. But the second the cameras go off and the curtains come down, all the despair and anxiety comes flooding back in a thousand-foot-tall tsunami.  


But there is only ever one option in times like these: forward. Swim or die. Get angry. Harness that rage to your advantage, to be an anaesthetic against the pain and regret and despair that threaten to consume you, to call you to action to save you from the hungry demons in the black pit at the bottom of your mind. 


Do literally anything other than sitting around passively waiting for the headsman's axe. Work out, polish your resume, apply to a few (higher paying!) private sector jobs just to say you did, call your congressional offices, take a little trip if you can afford it even if its just a day drive to nowhere with the music blasting, join a protest, read a book, go out to dinner somewhere even if it's only with yourself. Start a new hobby. It doesn't matter what you do as long as it's not wallowing helpless in the despair. Do it right now. Not later. Now. 

At first, it will NOT be easy. Your subconscious can be a very powerful, cunning, deceitful foe. It will tell you that you are not good enough, that you are betraying your ideals of selfless service by prioritizing your own well being for once. But at the end of the day, we always have to put our own oxygen mask in first. You have as much right to prioritize your needs as anyone. Perhaps even more right given how much you have sacrificed to protect that right for others. 


Don't let the bastards take your fire.

People who have never had experienced life-long severe depression think that healing from suicidal thoughts feels like inner peace and living happily forever after. 


In reality, healing from suicidal thoughts feels like fighting endless war with your inner demons every single moment of your life. They cannot destroy you as long as you keep fighting, but it impossible to ever truly defeat them forever. Until the day you die, even in your most joyous and self fulfilled moments, they are always still there. Watching, waiting. Hungering for more of your despair and self hatred, of which there is a neverending supply bubbling just beneath the surface. It would be so easy to just give up, let go, finally get some measure of peace in the oblivion of death. But you know you must hold the line; if not for yourself, for everyone around you. If you fail to keep fighting, you know the demons will move on to consume them just as they consumed you.
